faq.q: What is Brutalist architecture?
faq.a: Brutalist architecture uses exposed, unpainted concrete or brick, and treats honest materials as an ethic as much as a look. The name is often traced to béton brut, Le Corbusier's phrase for his rough concrete. Swedish architect Hans Asplund coined the word nybrutalism for a brick house designed in 1950, Alison Smithson first printed "new brutalism" in 1953, and the critic Reyner Banham used it in a 1955 essay.

faq.q: What are the key features of Brutalism?
faq.a: The defining material is exposed, unpainted concrete or brick. Many brutalist buildings also show their structure and circulation openly. Park Hill in Sheffield runs wide deck "streets in the sky" along its slabs, Balfron Tower in London puts its lifts in a separate tower linked to the flats by bridges every third floor, and Boston City Hall is an inverted ziggurat whose form shows the city government's work from outside.

faq.q: Which brutalist buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Start with Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation in Marseille (1952), often cited as the style's first inspiration: a vertical neighbourhood of duplex flats on internal streets. Then compare Park Hill in Sheffield (1961), Habitat 67 in Montréal (1967), with its stacked prefabricated modules, Denys Lasdun's Royal National Theatre in London (1976) and the Barbican Estate (1982), a walkway city of housing, arts centre and lake above the street.

faq.q: Where can I see brutalist buildings?
faq.a: The style spread to regions around the world, so there is brutalism on every continent. London has the Barbican, Trellick Tower and the Royal National Theatre; Boston has its City Hall; Le Corbusier's Capitol Complex stands in Chandigarh, India. Further afield are the Kenyatta International Convention Centre in Nairobi, the Bank of London and South America in Buenos Aires and the Museum of Modern Art in Rio de Janeiro.

faq.q: What is modernist architecture?
faq.a: Modernist architecture builds with new construction technology and rejects ornament, so volume, structure and plan carry the design. It emerged at the end of the 19th century and was dominant from the Second World War until the 1980s. Under the name International Style it spread throughout the world. Le Corbusier's white houses of the 1920s, for example, had no ornament inside or out.

faq.q: What are the principles of modernist architecture?
faq.a: In 1932 Hitchcock and Johnson's exhibition at MoMA in New York named three: architecture as volume, regularity in the facade rather than symmetry, and no applied ornament. You can see them at work in Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye (1931), which puts his Five Points of Architecture into one house, and in the Barcelona Pavilion (1929), where free-standing walls under a floating roof let space flow.

faq.q: Which modernist buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: A short list runs in date order: the Fagus Factory in Alfeld (1911), whose glass wall turns the corners with no column; Bauhaus Dessau (1926), with its pinwheel plan; the Barcelona Pavilion (1929); Villa Savoye (1931); Fallingwater (1939), cantilevered over a waterfall; and the Seagram Building in New York (1958), set back behind a plaza with bronze mullions that express the frame.

faq.q: Which modernist houses should I study?
faq.a: Houses show modernism's ideas most clearly. Compare the Rietveld Schröder House in Utrecht (1924), De Stijl in three dimensions; Villa Tugendhat in Brno (1930), whose glass walls drop away to the garden; Fallingwater (1939); the Eames House in Los Angeles (1949), built from off-the-shelf industrial parts; Philip Johnson's Glass House (1949); and the Farnsworth House (1951), a single glass room lifted above a floodplain.

faq.q: What is contemporary architecture?
faq.a: Contemporary architecture is the architecture of the 21st century, from 2000 to today, and no single style leads it. It is shaped by method more than style, and it is global, with important new buildings in China, Russia and India as well as Europe and the Americas. Examples range from Snøhetta's Oslo Opera House (2008) to OMA's CCTV Headquarters in Beijing (2012).

faq.q: What are the features of contemporary architecture?
faq.a: New structural systems let buildings be taller, lighter and stronger than in the 20th century, and designs are modelled in 3D on computers. Some designers favour natural, ecological materials, and energy efficiency over a building's whole life is a primary goal of sustainable design. Shigeru Ban's Centre Pompidou-Metz, for example, roofs its galleries with a woven grid of glued laminated timber.

faq.q: Which contemporary buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Good starting points are Toyo Ito's Sendai Mediatheque (2001), where thirteen lattice tubes carry thin floors; OMA's Seattle Central Library (2004), with its book spiral as one continuous ramp; Tate Modern in London (2000), a power station turned museum; the Oslo Opera House (2008); and Herzog & de Meuron's Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg (2017), a glass crown on a brick warehouse.

faq.q: Where can I see contemporary architecture?
faq.a: Almost anywhere, because the field is global. In Asia and the Middle East there are the CCTV Headquarters in Beijing, the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, once the tallest building in the world, and Foster + Partners' Queen Alia International Airport in Amman. In Europe, see Casa da Música in Porto or the Markthal in Rotterdam; in North America, the High Line in New York.

faq.q: What is deconstructivist architecture?
faq.a: Deconstructivist architecture breaks a building into fragments, with no obvious harmony, continuity or symmetry; its look is often described as controlled chaos. The name plays on Russian Constructivism and on the ideas of the French philosopher Jacques Derrida. The style came to public notice with the 1982 competition for the Parc de la Villette in Paris, and a 1988 exhibition at MoMA crystallised the movement.

faq.q: Who are the main deconstructivist architects?
faq.a: The 1988 MoMA exhibition, curated by Mark Wigley and Philip Johnson, made seven architects famous: Peter Eisenman, Frank Gehry, Zaha Hadid, Coop Himmelblau, Rem Koolhaas, Daniel Libeskind and Bernard Tschumi. The label does not fit all of them comfortably: Gehry refused it, as he refused any other, even though his Guggenheim Bilbao (1997) and Walt Disney Concert Hall (2003) are often shown as examples.

faq.q: Which deconstructivist buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Compare Eisenman's Wexner Center for the Arts in Columbus (1989), Gehry's Vitra Design Museum (1989) and Hadid's first built work, the Vitra Fire Station (1993), both in Weil am Rhein. Then study Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin (2001), a zigzag plan cut through by voids you can see but not enter, and his Imperial War Museum North in Manchester (2002), built from fragmented, intersecting curved volumes.

faq.q: Where can I see deconstructivist buildings?
faq.a: Germany has a cluster: the Vitra Design Museum and Vitra Fire Station in Weil am Rhein, BMW Welt in Munich, and the Jewish Museum Berlin. Frank Gehry's work is spread widely, from the Guggenheim Bilbao and the Dancing House in Prague to the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles and the Biomuseo in Panama City. In Rotterdam, OMA's Kunsthal threads ramps through a box.

faq.q: What is parametric architecture?
faq.a: Parametric architecture designs buildings with algorithms: the architect sets input parameters, and the model changes as they change. In parametricism every element of a design can vary and adapt to the others. It rejects both serial repetition and a heap of unrelated pieces, aiming for complex space that stays legible. Patrik Schumacher coined the term in 2008 and described it as a successor to modernism and postmodernism.

faq.q: How does parametric design work?
faq.a: The architect writes rules rather than drawing each part: an algorithm takes input parameters, and the model updates whenever one changes, so every element can adapt to the others. Grasshopper, a visual programming tool built on Rhino, is one tool for such models. The Canton Tower in Guangzhou (2010) shows the idea: a lattice of inclined steel columns twisted between two rotated ellipses.

faq.q: Who are the main parametric architects?
faq.a: Patrik Schumacher, who named parametricism, worked with Zaha Hadid, whose office designed many of the best-known examples, from MAXXI in Rome (2010) to the Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku (2012). Early practitioners also included Greg Lynn, Jesse Reiser, Lars Spuybroek and Kas Oosterhuis. On the wall you will also find UNStudio, J. Mayer H. and Studio Fuksas.

faq.q: What are good examples of parametric architecture?
faq.a: Study Zaha Hadid's Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku (2012), one continuous surface folding from plaza to roof; UNStudio's Mercedes-Benz Museum in Stuttgart (2006), with double-helix ramps on a trefoil plan; J. Mayer H.'s Metropol Parasol in Seville (2011), giant timber parasols over a market; and Studio Fuksas's Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport Terminal 3 (2013), wrapped in a double honeycomb skin.

faq.q: What is high-tech architecture?
faq.a: High-tech architecture shows how a building is made and how it works: structure, lifts, stairs and ducts are put on display instead of hidden. It emerged in the 1970s as a form of late modernism and was first developed in Britain. Steel, aluminium and glass dominate, and the style is used most for factories, offices and galleries.

faq.q: What are the key features of high-tech architecture?
faq.a: Interiors have no internal load-bearing walls, so the space can be rearranged, and services such as stairs and lifts often move outside into separate towers. The Lloyd's Building in London (1986) sets its lifts, stairs and ducts in plug-in towers around a 60-metre atrium, and the HSBC Main Building in Hong Kong (1986) hangs its floors from suspension trusses, freeing a public plaza beneath.

faq.q: Who are the main high-tech architects?
faq.a: The leading names are Michael and Patty Hopkins, Norman Foster, Richard Rogers, Renzo Piano and Santiago Calatrava. Many early leaders were British. Their key works on the wall include the Hopkins House in London (1976), Piano and Rogers's Centre Pompidou in Paris (1977), Foster's 30 St Mary Axe in London (2004) and Calatrava's Museum of Tomorrow in Rio de Janeiro (2015).

faq.q: Which high-tech buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Begin with the Centre Pompidou in Paris (1977), which moves structure and colour-coded services outside and leaves free floors and a public piazza. Then compare the Lloyd's Building (1986), the HSBC Main Building (1986), Renzo Piano's New York Times Building (2007), screened by ceramic rods, and Ken Yeang's Menara Mesiniaga in Malaysia (1992), which cools a round tower with sky gardens.

faq.q: What is postmodern architecture?
faq.a: Postmodern architecture brings back what modernism took out: historical references, ornament, colour and wit. It emerged in the 1960s as a reaction against the austerity and sameness of modern buildings. Denise Scott Brown and Robert Venturi are credited with introducing it, and Venturi set it out in a 1966 book that declared, "I am for messy vitality over obvious unity." In the late 1990s it split into many new tendencies.

faq.q: What are the key features of postmodern architecture?
faq.a: Postmodern buildings borrow historical elements and allusions and use unusual materials. Robert Venturi's Vanna Venturi House in Philadelphia (1964) splits a gable facade over a broken arch. Michael Graves's Portland Building (1982) paints giant pilasters and a keystone onto a cubic block, and the AT&T Building in New York (1984), by Philip Johnson and John Burgee, caps a granite tower with a broken pediment.

faq.q: Which postmodern buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Charles Moore's Piazza d'Italia in New Orleans (1978), a public square with a fountain shaped like Italy, is among the most famous works. Add the Vanna Venturi House (1964), the Portland Building (1982), James Stirling's Neue Staatsgalerie in Stuttgart (1984), which ramps a public path through a drum courtyard, and Venturi, Scott Brown and Associates' Sainsbury Wing at the National Gallery in London (1991).

faq.q: Was postmodern architecture only American?
faq.a: It is best known as an American style, but notable examples appeared in Europe and beyond. In Europe there are Ricardo Bofill's Walden 7 near Barcelona (1975), Piet Blom's Cube Houses in Rotterdam (1984), Hans Hollein's Haas House in Vienna (1990) and Aldo Rossi's Bonnefanten Museum in Maastricht (1995). In Asia, Taipei 101 (2004) stacks eight pagoda-like modules, and Kenzo Tange's Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building (1991) splits into twin towers.

faq.q: What is Art Deco architecture?
faq.a: Art Deco architecture pairs bold geometry with rich decoration: setbacks, sunbursts, metal ornament and decorated crowns. It first appeared in Paris in the 1910s, just before the First World War, growing from the geometric forms of the Vienna Secession and Cubism. Its name comes from the 1925 exhibition of decorative and industrial arts in Paris. It was an international style that flourished in the 1920s and early 1930s.

faq.q: What are the key features of Art Deco buildings?
faq.a: Look for bold geometry paired with rich decoration: stepped setbacks, sunbursts, metal ornament and decorated crowns. Reinforced concrete gave architects more freedom of form. The Chrysler Building in New York (1930) stacks a stainless-steel crown of sunburst arches above its setbacks, Radio City Music Hall (1932) shapes its auditorium ceiling from nested semicircles, and the Adler Planetarium in Chicago (1930) is a twelve-sided block in rainbow granite.

faq.q: Which Art Deco buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: The best-known skyscraper monuments are the Chrysler Building (1930) and the Empire State Building (1931) in New York. Before them, Auguste Perret's Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris (1913) spans its auditorium with a concrete frame behind a flat marble front. Then compare the Fisher Building in Detroit (1928), with its barrel-vaulted arcade, and the stepped Kavanagh building in Buenos Aires (1936).

faq.q: Where can I see Art Deco architecture?
faq.a: Miami Beach has the world's largest concentration of Art Deco buildings, and New York has its skyscrapers, from 30 Rockefeller Plaza to 70 Pine Street. Because the style was international, examples reach far beyond: the Parliament House in Helsinki, the Manila Metropolitan Theater with its Philippine plant motifs, the Australian War Memorial in Canberra and the Estadio Centenario in Montevideo, built for the first World Cup.

faq.q: What is Art Nouveau architecture?
faq.a: Art Nouveau architecture takes its lines from nature: the curves of plants and flowers, asymmetry and whiplash lines that give a sense of movement. The first Art Nouveau houses appeared in Brussels in the 1890s, and the style spread from Britain, Belgium and France across Europe. In German it is called Jugendstil, after the art journal Jugend. By the start of the First World War in 1914 it was largely exhausted.

faq.q: What materials did Art Nouveau architects use?
faq.a: They used the new materials of their time: iron, glass, ceramics and, later, concrete. Victor Horta's Hôtel Tassel in Brussels, a defining example, lets exposed iron columns and whiplash ornament flow through a top-lit stair hall. Otto Wagner's Majolikahaus in Vienna (1899) covers a flat apartment front in weatherproof tiles printed with flowers, and Hector Guimard brought the style to the street with his Paris Métro entrances.

faq.q: Which Art Nouveau buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Begin in Brussels with Victor Horta's Hôtel Tassel and Horta House (1901), then Josef Hoffmann's Stoclet Palace (1911). In Glasgow, Charles Rennie Mackintosh's Glasgow School of Art (1909) sets huge north-light studio windows in a stone front. In Barcelona, Antoni Gaudí's Casa Batlló (1906) and Casa Milà (1912) show the style at its most sculptural, and Eliel Saarinen's Helsinki Central Station (1919) shows its late, granite form.

faq.q: Is Gaudí's work Art Nouveau?
faq.a: On this site it is grouped with Art Nouveau, the movement of his time. Gaudí's buildings share its natural forms and movement but push them into structure: the Sagrada Família, begun in 1882, uses branching tree-like columns and hyperboloid vaults, and the Crypt of Colonia Güell (1914) has leaning columns and vaults found with a hanging model. Park Güell (1914) edges a terrace with a serpentine tiled bench.

faq.q: What is critical regionalism in architecture?
faq.a: Critical regionalism is modern architecture rooted in its place: it starts from the local topography, climate and light rather than a universal style. It tries to mediate between the global and the local languages of architecture, and it rejects the whimsy and ornament of postmodernism. The theorists Alexander Tzonis and Liane Lefaivre first presented the idea in 1981, and the historian Kenneth Frampton developed it further.

faq.q: What are the key features of regionalist architecture?
faq.a: Frampton stressed topography, climate and light, so regionalist buildings answer their site rather than a style. Álvaro Siza's Boa Nova Tea House (1963) sets low tiled roofs among the rocks above the sea. Renzo Piano's Jean-Marie Tjibaou Cultural Centre in Nouméa (1998) sets ten curved timber-ribbed cases that recall Kanak huts, their double skins venting the trade winds, and Luis Barragán's house in Mexico City (1948) turns a blank wall to the street and works with colour and light.

faq.q: Which regionalist buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Jørn Utzon's Bagsværd Church near Copenhagen (1976) is a cited example: a billowing concrete ceiling, washed with daylight, inside a plain industrial shell. Compare Siza's Boa Nova Tea House (1963) and Leça Swimming Pools (1966), Geoffrey Bawa's Parliament of Sri Lanka (1982), set on an island in a lake, and Balkrishna Doshi's Indian Institute of Management Bangalore (1983), with corridors under open pergolas.

faq.q: Who are the main regionalist architects?
faq.a: Critical regionalism has grown into distinct sub-styles around the world, so its architects come from many places: Jørn Utzon in Denmark, Álvaro Siza in Portugal, Luis Barragán in Mexico, Geoffrey Bawa in Sri Lanka, and Balkrishna Doshi and Charles Correa in India, whose Jawahar Kala Kendra in Jaipur (1991) is laid out on a nine-square plan.

faq.q: What makes good museum architecture?
faq.a: A museum has to keep a collection safe and open it to the public, and every museum building strikes its own balance between the two. Study how visitors move, where light comes from and what the museum does for its city. Louis Kahn's Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth (1972) lights its galleries through a slot in cycloid vaults; the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York (1959) is one spiral ramp.

faq.q: Which museums should architecture students study?
faq.a: Start with the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York (1959), called a landmark of 20th-century architecture. Then compare Mies van der Rohe's Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin (1968), one column-free glass hall; the Kimbell Art Museum (1972); Carlo Scarpa's Castelvecchio Museum in Verona (1975); Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao (1997); Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin (2001); and SANAA's 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa (2004).

faq.q: What is the Bilbao effect?
faq.a: Cities have long used museums as tools for economic growth. Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao opened in 1997, its titanium curves shaped with CATIA, software from the aerospace industry, and its pull on the city became known as the Bilbao effect. For students, it is a case study in what a museum does for its city as well as for its collection.

faq.q: What are good examples of museums in old buildings?
faq.a: Some museums move into buildings that have outlived their use; others marry a new wing to an old one. Tate Modern in London (2000) turned a power station into a museum, its Turbine Hall an indoor street. Carlo Scarpa reworked a medieval castle as the Castelvecchio Museum in Verona (1975), and I. M. Pei's Louvre Pyramid in Paris (1989) lights an underground hall that links the old museum's wings.

faq.q: Which famous houses should architecture students study?
faq.a: A core list: Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House in Chicago (1910) and Fallingwater (completed 1937); the Rietveld Schröder House in Utrecht (1924); Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye in Poissy, built 1928 to 1931; Mies van der Rohe's Villa Tugendhat (1930) and Farnsworth House (1951); Alvar Aalto's Villa Mairea (1939); the Eames House (1949); and Robert Venturi's Vanna Venturi House (1964).

faq.q: Why are houses important in architecture?
faq.a: Houses are small buildings that carry big arguments. A house can express the opinions of the people who build it or live in it, and its form is shaped by the materials at hand, so a single house can set out a whole way of building. Villa Savoye, built in reinforced concrete, puts Le Corbusier's Five Points of Architecture into one house and had an enormous influence on modernism.

faq.q: What were the Case Study Houses?
faq.a: In January 1945 John Entenza's magazine Arts & Architecture announced the Case Study Houses, a programme to produce inexpensive modern model homes that could be built again and again. The best known is the Eames House in Los Angeles, built in 1949 by Charles and Ray Eames for themselves from mass-produced parts.

faq.q: What are the most famous modernist glass houses?
faq.a: Mies van der Rohe's Farnsworth House in Plano (1951) is a single glass room lifted above a floodplain on eight steel columns, a glass and steel box in the International Style. Philip Johnson's Glass House in New Canaan (1949) is a glass box whose walls are the landscape; only the bathroom is enclosed. Earlier, Mies's Villa Tugendhat in Brno (1930) has glass walls that drop away to the garden.

faq.q: What makes good library architecture?
faq.a: A library has to store books and bring people to them, and over time the balance has moved from archive to public room. Today libraries also work as community hubs. Helsinki Central Library Oodi (2018) bridges an open ground floor with a spruce-clad timber wave, under a top-floor reading room called book heaven, while Dokk1 in Aarhus (2015) combines library and citizens' services on the waterfront.

faq.q: Which libraries should architecture students study?
faq.a: Begin with Henri Labrouste's Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève in Paris, opened in 1851, called a major step towards modern architecture for its exposed cast-iron columns and arches. Then compare Gunnar Asplund's Stockholm Public Library (1928), Alvar Aalto's Viipuri Library (1935), lit by round conical skylights, the Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library (1963), the Geisel Library in San Diego (1970) and Mecanoo's Library of Birmingham (2013).

faq.q: How has library design changed over time?
faq.a: The first libraries, such as the Library of Ashurbanipal in Mesopotamia, were archives of early writing. As collections grew, libraries ran short of space and introduced compact shelving on tracks. Between 1883 and 1929, 1,689 Carnegie libraries were built in the United States, and the public libraries of the 1960s were shaped by modernism. Recent libraries add public rooms, from Oodi in Helsinki to Calgary Central Library (2018).

faq.q: What are good examples of modern libraries?
faq.a: Alberto Kalach's Vasconcelos Library in Mexico City (2006) hangs steel book stacks in a tall glazed hall within a botanical garden. Snøhetta's Bibliotheca Alexandrina (2002) lights a terraced reading room through a tilted disc roof, behind a granite wall of scripts. Mecanoo's Library of Birmingham (2013) stacks boxes wrapped in interlocking metal rings, with a rotunda reading room and garden terraces, and Oodi in Helsinki (2018) opens its ground floor to the city.

faq.q: What is a pavilion in architecture?
faq.a: A pavilion is a smaller building set apart from, or attached to, a main building, and it was traditionally built for pleasure and relaxation. The word comes from a large tent raised on posts. Today the word also covers the national pavilions of world's fairs and art biennales, most of them temporary and taken down when the fair closes.

faq.q: Why are pavilions important in architecture?
faq.a: Because they are small and often temporary, pavilions let architects test an idea in full size. Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich's Barcelona Pavilion (1929) sets free-standing walls under a floating roof, so space flows instead of forming rooms. At Expo 2000 in Hanover, Shigeru Ban's Japan Pavilion was a gridshell of recycled paper tubes, and Buckminster Fuller's Montreal Biosphère (1967) is a steel-tube geodesic dome.

faq.q: What is the Serpentine Pavilion?
faq.a: Since 2000 the Serpentine Galleries in London have commissioned a temporary summer pavilion from a leading architect every year. Like most fair pavilions, each one is taken down at the end of its season, so it works as a full-size test of an architect's ideas. For a permanent counterpart, the Giardini in Venice holds 30 national pavilions, some by leading 20th-century architects, such as Sverre Fehn's Nordic Pavilion (1962).

faq.q: Which world's fair pavilions should architecture students study?
faq.a: Compare the Barcelona Pavilion (1929); the Atomium in Brussels (1958), nine steel spheres in an iron-crystal pattern; the Montreal Biosphère (1967); Álvaro Siza's Portugal Pavilion in Lisbon (1998), whose thin concrete canopy hangs like a sheet between two porticoes; MVRDV's Netherlands Pavilion, Expo 2000, a vertical park of stacked Dutch landscapes; and He Jingtang's China Pavilion, Expo 2010, modelled on dougong timber brackets.

faq.q: What is social housing in architecture?
faq.a: Public or social housing is subsidised or affordable housing, usually provided in larger buildings. Modern municipal housing began as a response to fast urban population growth. In Britain, mass council house building began around 1920, after the Addison Act of 1919, and tower blocks followed in the 1950s. In Vienna, the Red Vienna programme placed large blocks such as the Karl-Marx-Hof (1930) around green courts.

faq.q: Which housing projects should architecture students study?
faq.a: In date order: Bruno Taut and Martin Wagner's Hufeisensiedlung in Berlin (1927), a horseshoe around a pond; the Weissenhof Estate in Stuttgart (1927); the Karl-Marx-Hof in Vienna (1930); Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation in Marseille (1952); Park Hill in Sheffield (1961); Habitat 67 in Montréal (1967); the Barbican Estate in London (1982); and Alejandro Aravena's Quinta Monroy in Iquique, Chile (2004).

faq.q: What does "streets in the sky" mean?
faq.a: It describes housing where wide access corridors or decks work like streets above the ground. Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation in Marseille (1952) has 337 flats, with internal streets on every third floor and a shared terrace on the flat roof. Park Hill in Sheffield (1961) takes those streets outside as wide concrete decks that follow the slope, and Balfron Tower in London (1967) links its flats to a separate service tower by bridges.

faq.q: What is incremental housing?
faq.a: Incremental housing builds part of a home well and lets residents finish the rest as they can. Alejandro Aravena's Quinta Monroy in Iquique, Chile (2004) built half a good house for each family and left the other half for them to complete; the approach helped Aravena win the 2016 Pritzker Prize. It is a useful precedent for any student project on affordable housing.

faq.q: What is sacred architecture?
faq.a: Sacred or religious architecture is the design and building of places of worship, whose plan and form carry belief. Ancient temples were often seen as a god's dwelling, and a Hindu temple is read as a model of the universe and of inner space, its sanctum crowned by a tower, the shikhara, called the vimana in the south. Bahá'í houses of worship are nine-sided, with nine entrances.

faq.q: How did mosque architecture develop?
faq.a: The earliest mosques were hypostyle halls, pioneered under the Umayyads, with a courtyard for Friday prayer crowds. The Ottomans introduced the central-dome mosque in the 15th century: Mimar Sinan's Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul (1557) buttresses its dome with half-domes, and the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne (1575) carries one wide dome on eight piers. Modern mosques reinterpret both, like Marina Tabassum's Bait Ur Rouf Mosque in Dhaka (2012).

faq.q: Which religious buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Hagia Sophia in Istanbul (537) was one of the first buildings with a fully pendentive dome. The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali (1907) is built of mud brick, its palm-wood beams left as fixed scaffolding. Then compare Le Corbusier's Notre-Dame du Haut in Ronchamp (1955), Oscar Niemeyer's Cathedral of Brasília (1970), Tadao Ando's Church of the Light (1989) and the Lotus Temple in New Delhi (1986).

faq.q: How did modern materials change church design?
faq.a: Gothic architecture, which began in 12th-century France at the abbey church of Saint-Denis, was defined by the pointed arch. In the 20th century, steel and concrete changed church design. Kenzo Tange's St. Mary's Cathedral in Tokyo (1964) meets eight hyperbolic paraboloid shells in a cross-shaped skylight, Niemeyer's Cathedral of Brasília rings a sunken nave with sixteen curved concrete columns, and Ando cuts a cross of light into a concrete wall.

faq.q: Why does school architecture matter?
faq.a: The design of a building can strongly shape how students learn, so a school's plan, light and shared spaces are part of its teaching. In the late 1960s and 1970s open classrooms became popular in North America. SANAA's Rolex Learning Center in Lausanne (2010) takes the idea further: one continuous floor rises and falls as hills and valleys, pierced by patios, in place of stairs and walls.

faq.q: What is the difference between an American campus and a British university?
faq.a: A campus traditionally means the land and buildings of a college or university. In 1922 Patrick Abercrombie contrasted the American campus, its departments scattered about a park among the trees, with the formal quadrangles of Oxford and Cambridge. Gothic, which flourished in English universities from the 13th to the 15th centuries, was later revived for campuses, as in Pittsburgh's Cathedral of Learning (1937).

faq.q: Which school and campus buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar on 1 April 1919, and his Bauhaus Dessau (1926) wraps the workshops in a glass curtain wall on a pinwheel plan. Then compare Mackintosh's Glasgow School of Art (1909), Mies's S. R. Crown Hall in Chicago (1956), Le Corbusier's Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts (1963), Louis Kahn's Phillips Exeter Academy Library (1971) and Herzog & de Meuron's Blavatnik School of Government in Oxford (2015).

faq.q: Why are so many university buildings brutalist?
faq.a: Brutalism was widely used on university campuses around the world in the 1960s and 1970s. Paul Rudolph's Yale Art and Architecture Building (1963) is a design studio built in section, with dozens of interlocking levels. Vilanova Artigas's FAU-USP in São Paulo (1969) puts an architecture school under one great roof, joined by ramps, and Denys Lasdun's ziggurats at the University of East Anglia (1968) step down to a lake.

faq.q: What is memorial architecture?
faq.a: A memorial is an object or place that focuses memory or commemoration, and memorial architecture gives remembering a place. The most common kind is a gravestone or a plaque; temporary, makeshift memorials are called grassroots memorials. A mausoleum is a monument that encloses a burial chamber: the word comes from the tomb of Mausolus at Halicarnassus. Anitkabir in Ankara (1953), the mausoleum of Atatürk, is one modern example.

faq.q: Which memorials should architecture students study?
faq.a: Compare the Taj Mahal in Agra (1653), a white marble tomb on a raised plinth in a quartered garden; Eero Saarinen's Gateway Arch in St. Louis (1965); Enric Miralles and Carme Pinós's Igualada Cemetery (1994), a path cut into a former quarry; Peter Eisenman's Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe in Berlin (2005); and Michael Arad and Peter Walker's National September 11 Memorial in New York (2011).

faq.q: Why was the Vietnam Veterans Memorial controversial?
faq.a: Maya Lin's Vietnam Veterans Memorial, dedicated in 1982, is two black granite walls. Its colour, its lack of ornament and its form set below the ground were controversial at first. It is a useful case for students because each of those three choices, material, decoration and section, is what gives the memorial its meaning, and each was what critics first objected to.

faq.q: How does the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe work?
faq.a: Peter Eisenman's memorial in Berlin, opened in 2005, sets 2,711 concrete stelae of varying height on a sloping grid, forming narrow aisles that visitors walk between. There are no names or information on the stelae themselves, and critics have said that this weakens its message. Compare it with the National September 11 Memorial, where two square voids mark the towers' footprints.

faq.q: Why is London's architecture worth studying?
faq.a: London has been rebuilt again and again on its old ground. The Great Fire of 1666, which destroyed about nine tenths of the city, was a turning point: Wren's grid plan was set aside, and the city was rebuilt on its medieval streets under a 1667 act asking for brick houses of uniform height and plot size. Victorian London then built the world's first underground railway.

faq.q: Which modern buildings in London should architecture students visit?
faq.a: A good route takes in Denys Lasdun's Royal National Theatre (1976), whose concrete terraces step toward the Thames; the Barbican Estate (1982); Richard Rogers's Lloyd's Building (1986); Tate Modern (2000), a power station turned museum; Foster and Partners' 30 St Mary Axe (2004), a diagrid tower; and Renzo Piano's The Shard (2012), London's first supertall skyscraper.

faq.q: Where can I see brutalist architecture in London?
faq.a: London has some of the best-known brutalist buildings anywhere. The Barbican Estate and Barbican Centre (1982) lift housing, an arts centre and a lake onto walkways above the street. Ernő Goldfinger's Balfron Tower (1967) and Trellick Tower (1972) put their lifts in separate towers linked to the flats by bridges every third floor, and the Royal National Theatre (1976) sits on the South Bank.

faq.q: Which historic buildings in London should architecture students know?
faq.a: Wren's dome for St Paul's Cathedral was praised by Pevsner as among the most perfect in the world. John Nash laid out Regent Street with James Burton and remodelled Buckingham House into Buckingham Palace. Sir John Soane's Museum (1824) draws daylight down through narrow, layered rooms, and the Palace of Westminster (1876), by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin, wraps parliament in Perpendicular Gothic Revival detail.

faq.q: Why is New York's architecture worth studying?
faq.a: New York has one of the largest and most varied collections of skyscrapers in the world, and its rules shaped them. The 1916 Zoning Resolution required setbacks and limited towers to a share of the lot, and Art Deco towers such as the Chrysler and Empire State buildings took their tapered tops from those rules. Grand Central Terminal was built in the Beaux-Arts style.

faq.q: Which skyscrapers in New York should architecture students study?
faq.a: In date order: the Flatiron Building (1902), filling a triangular block; Cass Gilbert's Woolworth Building (1913), a steel frame in Gothic Revival terracotta; the Chrysler Building (1930), which many historians and architects rank among the city's finest; the Empire State Building (1931), the first to pass 100 storeys; the Seagram Building (1958); and Herzog & de Meuron's 56 Leonard Street (2017).

faq.q: Which modern buildings in New York should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Frank Lloyd Wright's Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum (1959) replaces floors with one spiral ramp. Mies van der Rohe's Seagram Building (1958) stands back behind a plaza; the critic Paul Goldberger called it one of the city's most copied buildings. Add Eero Saarinen's TWA Flight Center (1962), the Ford Foundation Building (1967), with its glazed garden atrium, and the High Line (2009), a railway turned park.

faq.q: What are the best examples of International Style buildings in New York?
faq.a: The Seagram Building and 330 West 42nd Street are named as early, influential examples of the International Style in the United States. On the wall you can compare the United Nations Headquarters (1952), a thin Secretariat slab with glass curtain-wall faces; SOM's Manufacturers Trust Company Building (1954), a glass-walled bank on Fifth Avenue; and the Seagram Building (1958), whose bronze mullions express the frame.

faq.q: Why is Chicago important in architecture?
faq.a: Chicago is where the skyscraper was worked out. After the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 destroyed most of downtown, the city rebuilt. The Montauk Building (1882–83) was the first to be called a skyscraper, and Jenney's Home Insurance Building (1885) is considered the first with steel in its structural frame. A steel skeleton meant height was no longer limited by the strength of the walls.

faq.q: What is the Chicago School of architecture?
faq.a: The Chicago School grew out of the city's rebuilding on steel frames, which freed height from the strength of the walls. Louis Sullivan set aside historical precedent to stress height. The Reliance Building (1895) was the first skyscraper with large plate-glass windows over most of its surface. From 1963 a "Second Chicago School" grew from Mies van der Rohe's work at IIT, where his S. R. Crown Hall (1956) stands.

faq.q: Which buildings in Chicago should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Start with Burnham & Root's Rookery Building (1888) and the Monadnock Building (1893), the tallest load-bearing masonry building ever built. Add Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House (1910); Mies's 860-880 Lake Shore Drive (1951), two steel and glass towers at right angles; Bruce Graham and Fazlur Khan's John Hancock Center (1969) and Willis Tower (1973); and Jeanne Gang's Aqua Tower (2009), whose balconies form undulating contours.

faq.q: Who were the most important Chicago architects?
faq.a: The key names start with Daniel Burnham, who led the design of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, the "White City", and with John Root built the Rookery and the Monadnock. Then Louis Sullivan, whose Sullivan Center sets a white terracotta grid over an ornate cast-iron base. Later came Mies van der Rohe, whose work at IIT started a Second Chicago School, and SOM's Bruce Graham and Fazlur Khan, who designed the John Hancock Center's X-braced tube.

faq.q: Why is Paris important in architecture?
faq.a: Paris is a city where styles were born. Gothic architecture began in the rebuilding of the choir of Saint-Denis, finished in 1144, and around 1160 Maurice de Sully used it at a far larger scale for Notre-Dame; the upper chapel of Sainte-Chapelle is called the supreme example of the new style. From 1546 the Louvre's Lescot wing was rebuilt in the French Renaissance style.

faq.q: How did Haussmann change Paris?
faq.a: In 1853 Napoleon III made Haussmann prefect of the Seine, starting the rebuilding of Paris; the programme ended when Haussmann was dismissed in January 1870. It built on older rules, because the city had imposed formal height limits on its buildings as early as 1667. Charles Garnier's Palais Garnier (1875) belongs to the same era.

faq.q: Which modern buildings in Paris should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers's Centre Pompidou (1977), chosen from 681 competition entries, moves its structure and colour-coded services outside. Compare I. M. Pei's Louvre Pyramid (1989), Bernard Tschumi's parc de la Villette (1987), a grid of red follies, Jean Nouvel's Fondation Cartier (1994) and Musée du quai Branly (2006), and Frank Gehry's Fondation Louis Vuitton (2014), with its twelve curved glass sails.

faq.q: What did the world's fairs leave in Paris?
faq.a: The world's fairs of 1889 and 1900 added the Eiffel Tower and the Grand Palais. Gustave Eiffel's tower (1889) gathers four curving wrought-iron legs into a single tapering shaft. Charles Girault's Grand Palais (1900) hides a riveted steel-and-glass vaulted nave behind stone Beaux-Arts facades, and his Petit Palais, from the same year, sets top-lit galleries around a semicircular garden court.

faq.q: Why is Berlin's architecture worth studying?
faq.a: Berlin's 20th century, from Weimar-era reform to the Cold War and after, is written in its buildings. East Berlin built Karl-Marx-Allee (1949–1960) as a showpiece of workers' housing in socialist classicism, while the Hansaviertel in the west was rebuilt as the Interbau project with Aalto, Gropius, Niemeyer and others. Potsdamer Platz, left desolate in the Cold War, was rebuilt in the 1990s.

faq.q: Which modern buildings in Berlin should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Start with Hans Scharoun's Berliner Philharmonie (1963), whose vineyard terraces of seats surround the orchestra, and Mies van der Rohe's Neue Nationalgalerie (1968), one column-free glass hall. Then see Norman Foster's Reichstag dome (1999), Daniel Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin (2001), a deconstructivist zigzag cut through by voids, Peter Eisenman's Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe (2005) and David Chipperfield's James Simon Gallery (2019).

faq.q: What are the Berlin Modernism Housing Estates?
faq.a: Seven housing estates from the Weimar years, by Bruno Taut, Martin Wagner and others, now form a World Heritage group, and they shaped housing design far beyond Germany. Taut's Gartenstadt Falkenberg (1916), nicknamed the paintbox estate, paints its garden-city terraces in strong colours, and Taut and Wagner's Hufeisensiedlung (1927) bends a horseshoe of housing around a pond.

faq.q: Who was Karl Friedrich Schinkel?
faq.a: Schinkel set Berlin's classical core. He drew the plans for the Altes Museum on Museum Island, opened in 1830 behind a colonnade of eighteen Ionic columns, and it became a model for national art museums elsewhere. His Bauakademie (1836, demolished 1962) is seen as a forerunner of modern architecture. Museum Island's other museums were built over a century, first under the Prussian kings.

faq.q: Why is Tokyo important for modern architecture?
faq.a: Tokyo's buildings share no single style, but the city is a key place to study modern Japanese architecture. It was left in ruins twice in recent history and rebuilt each time: the Great Kanto earthquake of 1923 began an era of concrete building, and an air raid in March 1945 burned much of the city. The 1964 Olympics marked its rebirth as a modern city.

faq.q: What is Metabolism in architecture?
faq.a: Metabolism was launched with a manifesto for the 1960 World Design Conference in Tokyo, and it treated the city as a living organism that renews itself. Kenzo Tange mentored the Metabolists without joining them. Kisho Kurokawa's Nakagin Capsule Tower (1972) bolts prefabricated capsules to two cores, the Metabolist idea of replaceable parts, and it pioneered capsule architecture.

faq.q: Which buildings in Tokyo should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Begin with Le Corbusier's National Museum of Western Art (1959) and Kenzo Tange's Yoyogi National Gymnasium (1964), whose suspension roof hangs from two concrete masts and which his Pritzker citation praised. Add Tange's St. Mary's Cathedral (1964), Fumihiko Maki's Spiral (1985), Rafael Viñoly's Tokyo International Forum (1996), Renzo Piano's Maison Hermès (2001) and Kengo Kuma's Japan National Stadium (2019).

faq.q: How do Tokyo's buildings deal with earthquakes?
faq.a: After the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake the city moved toward concrete construction. On the wall, Renzo Piano's Maison Hermès (2001) sets its glass-block skin on a frame designed to flex in earthquakes, and Nikken Sekkei's Tokyo Skytree (2012) uses a concrete core as a damping column, like the central column of a pagoda, as its triangular base turns into a round plan.

faq.q: Why is Barcelona important in architecture?
faq.a: Barcelona is studied for one plan and one movement. Ildefons Cerdà's Eixample of 1859, the city's biggest expansion, laid a grid of wide avenues and blocks with cut corners. Modernisme ran from the city's first World Fair in 1888 to 1911. Older layers survive too: the city began as the Roman town of Barcino, and the Gothic Quarter holds its oldest parts.

faq.q: Which Gaudí buildings should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Antoni Gaudí is Modernisme's best-known architect. See Casa Vicens (1885), his first major project; Palau Güell (1890), with a central hall under a perforated dome; Casa Batlló (1906), whose light well is tiled from deep to pale blue to even out the daylight; Casa Milà (1912), with its undulating stone facade; Park Güell (1914); and the Sagrada Familia, begun in 1882.

faq.q: Who was Domènech i Montaner?
faq.a: Lluís Domènech i Montaner was the Modernisme architect who offered a genuine alternative to Gaudí. His Palau de la Música Catalana (1908) uses a steel frame to open walls of glass and a stained-glass skylight over the concert hall. His Hospital de Sant Pau sets brick ward pavilions in gardens linked by underground service tunnels, so the hospital reads as a garden of small buildings.

faq.q: Which modern buildings in Barcelona should architecture students visit?
faq.a: The Barcelona Pavilion by Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich, built for the 1929 Exposition, was demolished in 1930 and rebuilt permanently in 1983–86. Then see Josep Lluís Sert's Fundació Joan Miró (1975), Arata Isozaki's Palau Sant Jordi (1990), Jean Nouvel's Torre Glòries (2005), Enric Ruiz-Geli's Media-TIC (2010), wrapped in ETFE cushions, and Lacol's La Borda (2018), cooperative housing in cross-laminated timber.

faq.q: What is Los Angeles architecture known for?
faq.a: Los Angeles mixes many styles, from Mission Revival onward, but it is studied above all for its modern houses. The Case Study Houses changed how American homes were designed. Googie, the roadside Space Age style, was named after a Hollywood coffee shop. In 1978 the Los Angeles Conservancy was founded to save the Central Library from demolition.

faq.q: Which Case Study Houses should architecture students know?
faq.a: Arts & Architecture launched the programme in 1945 and asked for houses that could be repeated, not one-off performances. Charles and Ray Eames's Eames House (1949) is assembled from off-the-shelf industrial parts. Pierre Koenig's Stahl House (Case Study House #22), from 1960, cantilevers an L-shaped steel and glass pavilion over the Hollywood Hills, and its photograph is one of the most famous of Los Angeles.

faq.q: Which modern houses in Los Angeles should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Begin with Frank Lloyd Wright's Hollyhock House (1921), which he called his "California Romanza", and Rudolph Schindler's house (1922), a live/work experiment for two families that set a precedent for California architecture. Then see Richard Neutra's Lovell Health House (1929), often called the first steel-frame house in the US, the Eames House (1949), John Lautner's Chemosphere (1960) and the Stahl House (1960).

faq.q: Which public buildings in Los Angeles should architecture students study?
faq.a: Frank Gehry's Walt Disney Concert Hall (2003) wraps a vineyard-style hall in curved stainless steel, swapped in for the stone first planned. Compare Richard Meier's Getty Center (1997), a hilltop campus on two shifted grids; Rafael Moneo's Cathedral of Our Lady of the Angels (2002), lit through alabaster windows; and Morphosis's Caltrans District 7 Headquarters (2004), an office slab in a perforated aluminium skin.

faq.q: What is adaptive reuse in architecture?
faq.a: Adaptive reuse gives an existing building a new purpose instead of pulling it down. It avoids the cost of demolition and keeps the energy already spent on the original building, and it keeps a community's link to its past. An old building can also be mined for materials for new projects. A classic example is Tate Modern in London, a gallery in a power station that opened in 2000.

faq.q: What are good examples of adaptive reuse?
faq.a: The Musée d'Orsay in Paris (1986) fills a former railway station. Lina Bo Bardi's SESC Pompéia in São Paulo (1986) keeps a drum factory as a leisure centre. Tate Modern's Turbine Hall became an indoor street, the High Line in New York (2009) is a park on an old elevated railway, and the Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg (2017) sets a glass crown on a brick warehouse.

faq.q: What are the challenges of adaptive reuse?
faq.a: The usual hurdles are the existing structure and building codes, so a condition survey decides whether a project works. The design then has to decide what to keep and where a new cut can open the old structure. Zeitz MOCAA in Cape Town (2017) carves a grain silo into an atrium shaped like a single grain of corn, and Peter Zumthor's Kolumba Museum (2007) builds a brick veil over a ruined Gothic church.

faq.q: How do architects add new parts to old buildings?
faq.a: Compare three approaches. Carlo Scarpa's Castelvecchio Museum in Verona (1975) reworks a medieval castle with precise new joints, cuts and display stands. OMA's Fondazione Prada in Milan (2015) joins former distillery buildings with new galleries and a tower. Zaha Hadid Architects' Port House in Antwerp (2016) hovers a faceted glass extension, shaped like a ship's bow, on concrete piers above an old fire station.

faq.q: What is a cantilever in architecture?
faq.a: A cantilever is a structural member fixed at one end and free at the other, so a building can overhang with no support underneath. In a traditional timber-framed building, a cantilevered upper floor is called a jetty, and bridges can be built outward from both sides as pairs of cantilevers that meet in the middle. Frank Lloyd Wright used cantilevers to push Fallingwater's large balconies over a waterfall.

faq.q: What are famous examples of cantilevers in architecture?
faq.a: Wright's Robie House in Chicago (1910) projects long roofs from the core instead of resting them on walls, and Fallingwater's concrete terraces are held only at one end, extending from the chimney. Giuseppe Pettazzi's Fiat Tagliero Building in Asmara (1938) cantilevers two 15 m concrete wings from a central tower, and OMA's CCTV Headquarters in Beijing (2012) joins two leaning towers with a 75-metre cantilever.

faq.q: Which building has the longest cantilever roof?
faq.a: Coop Himmelb(l)au's Busan Cinema Center in South Korea (2011) is captioned as having the world's longest cantilever roof, carried on a single cone over an outdoor theatre. Other long reaches on the wall include Moshe Safdie's Marina Bay Sands in Singapore (2010), whose sky park cantilevers far beyond the north tower, and Jean Nouvel's Guthrie Theater in Minneapolis (2006), with a long bridge reaching toward the Mississippi.

faq.q: How do cantilevers shape towers?
faq.a: In a tower the cantilever can come from the core rather than the walls. Wright's Price Tower (1956), his only built skyscraper, cantilevers its floors like branches from a central core. BBPR's Torre Velasca in Milan (1958) pushes its upper residential floors out on angled ribs, and Herzog & de Meuron's 56 Leonard Street in New York (2017) shifts and cantilevers its floor plates so each flat gets its own outline.

faq.q: What is a courtyard in architecture?
faq.a: A courtyard is an area open to the sky, often surrounded by a building. It brings light, air and privacy into the middle of a plan, which people want nearly everywhere, and in warm weather an open central court helps cool a house. Courtyard houses go back to the Neolithic, around 6400–6000 BC, and the open centre of a Roman house was called the atrium.

faq.q: What are good examples of courtyard architecture?
faq.a: In the Alhambra in Granada the basic unit of the palace is a rectangular courtyard. The Shah Mosque in Isfahan (1629) rings its central courtyard with four monumental iwans. Louis Kahn's Salk Institute (1965) sets its laboratories around a travertine plaza open to the Pacific, and Alvar Aalto's Säynätsalo Town Hall (1952) gathers brick rooms around a raised grass courtyard.

faq.q: Which courtyard houses should architecture students study?
faq.a: Courtyards were widely used in the ancient Middle East, and in Morocco's old towns the courtyard house has always been the standard form. For modern versions, compare Luis Barragán's house in Mexico City (1948), Alvar Aalto's Villa Mairea (1939), with its L-shaped courtyard, and Tadao Ando's Row House in Sumiyoshi (1976), whose interior courtyard brings in light and has to be crossed to get from room to room.

faq.q: How do contemporary buildings use courtyards?
faq.a: The courtyard still organises large plans. I. M. Pei's Suzhou Museum (2006) sets white walls around a water garden. OMA and Ole Scheeren's The Interlace in Singapore (2013) stacks thirty-one blocks in a hexagonal weave that forms large garden courtyards. Foster + Partners' Kogod Courtyard at the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C. (2007) covers a 19th-century courtyard with an undulating glass canopy.

faq.q: What is a brise-soleil?
faq.a: A brise-soleil, French for "sun breaker", is a screen that shades a facade and cuts a building's heat gain by deflecting sunlight. The simplest form is a horizontal projection on the sunny side. It is used most on glass facades that would otherwise overheat, and it still lets in the low sun of mornings, evenings and winter, so louvres can also help heat a building passively.

faq.q: How did Le Corbusier use the brise-soleil?
faq.a: Le Corbusier popularised patterned concrete versions. At Chandigarh his Palace of Assembly (1962) is a parliament built for the Punjab sun, the Secretariat Building (1958) runs a brise-soleil grid along a long concrete slab, and the Palace of Justice (1955) shades its courts under a huge concrete parasol roof. In Ahmedabad, the Mill Owners' Association Building (1954) uses angled concrete fins.

faq.q: What are good examples of brise-soleil in architecture?
faq.a: Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer's Gustavo Capanema Palace in Rio de Janeiro (1945) sets adjustable brise-soleil on an office slab, and Niemeyer's Copan Building in São Paulo (1966) runs continuous horizontal sunshades along a serpentine slab. Renzo Piano's New York Times Building (2007) screens its glass walls with ceramic rods, and David Chipperfield's Amorepacific Headquarters in Seoul (2017) wraps a near-cube in vertical sun screens.

faq.q: Can a brise-soleil move?
faq.a: Yes. Santiago Calatrava designed a moving one shaped like a wing: the Milwaukee Art Museum's Quadracci Pavilion (2001) opens and folds a winged sunscreen of steel fins above a glass hall. At the Institut du Monde Arabe in Paris, 240 photo-sensitive, motor-controlled apertures act as a brise-soleil, opening and closing to control the light that reaches the interior.

faq.q: What is mass timber?
faq.a: Mass timber is a class of large engineered wood parts that carry a building's structure. Cross-laminated timber (CLT), one kind, stacks layers of boards at right angles for strength and serves for walls, floors and roofs. Mass timber buildings go up faster than steel or concrete ones and perform very well in earthquakes. Lacol's La Borda in Barcelona (2018) is cooperative housing built in cross-laminated timber.

faq.q: What are good examples of timber architecture?
faq.a: Compare Alvar Aalto's Villa Mairea (1939), modernism softened with timber; E. Fay Jones's Thorncrown Chapel (1980), a lattice of small pine members sized to be carried by hand; Renzo Piano's Jean-Marie Tjibaou Cultural Centre (1998); Shigeru Ban's Centre Pompidou-Metz (2010), under a woven glulam grid; K2S's Kamppi Chapel in Helsinki (2012); and Kengo Kuma's Japan National Stadium (2019), with timber louvres from all 47 prefectures.

faq.q: What is the tallest wooden building?
faq.a: Voll Arkitekter's Mjøstårnet in Brumunddal, Norway, finished in 2019, was the world's tallest wooden building when it was completed: an 18-storey glulam frame. For the largest, J. Mayer H.'s Metropol Parasol in Seville (2011) is marketed as the world's largest wooden structure, spreading giant timber parasols over a market and Roman ruins, with a walkway on top.

faq.q: What are the oldest timber buildings?
faq.a: Building in wood is very old. The oldest known half-timbered building is in Roman Herculaneum. The Pagoda of Fogong Temple in Yingxian (1056) is the oldest fully wooden pagoda still standing in China, and the Ise Grand Shrine in Japan is traditionally rebuilt in cypress every 20 years, which keeps the craft alive. Kyoto's Katsura Imperial Villa (17th century) shows tatami-module rooms and sliding screens.

faq.q: What is a tensile structure?
faq.a: A tensile structure carries only tension, with no compression or bending, and it should not be confused with tensegrity. Because tensile structures span long distances economically, they are most often roofs, and pretensioning keeps their flexible parts stiff under load. Kenzo Tange's Yoyogi National Gymnasium in Tokyo (1964) hangs its roof from two concrete masts, and the Munich Olympic Stadium (1972) spreads a cable-net roof over its seating.

faq.q: Who was Frei Otto?
faq.a: Frei Otto championed tensile structures. He founded the Institute for Lightweight Structures in Stuttgart in 1964, first used a tensile roof for the West German pavilion at Expo 67, and then for the Munich Olympic Stadium (1972), designed with Behnisch & Partner, whose cable-net roof carries acrylic glass panels. An earlier pioneer, Vladimir Shukhov, was one of the first to calculate the stresses in such structures.

faq.q: What are good examples of tensile structures?
faq.a: Maciej Nowicki's J. S. Dorton Arena in Raleigh (1952) was the first structure in the world with a cable-supported roof. Then compare Eero Saarinen's Washington Dulles Airport Terminal (1962), whose concrete roof hangs in a catenary curve; the Yoyogi National Gymnasium (1964); SOM's Hajj Terminal in Jeddah (1981); Eduardo Souto de Moura's Braga Municipal Stadium (2003); and Hopkins Architects' London Velodrome (2011), a cable-net roof shaped like the track.

faq.q: What materials are used for tensile roofs?
faq.a: Common fabrics are PTFE-coated fibreglass and PVC-coated polyester, and some roofs use ETFE film in single layers or cushions. Richard Rogers's Millennium Dome in London (1999) hangs a PTFE-coated fabric roof on cables from twelve yellow masts. Shigeru Ban's Centre Pompidou-Metz (2010) stretches a PTFE membrane over a woven timber grid, and Foster + Partners' Khan Shatyr Entertainment Center in Astana (2010) is a tilted cable-net tent of ETFE cushions.
